items.claim: Argument stringification on every field pair slows validation 3-31x
items.consequence: This rule compares every pair of same-named fields, so its cost grows with the square of the number of repeated fields, and validation runs on untrusted client queries before execution. The old code exited after a length check for fields without arguments. Now each pair builds a synthetic ObjectValueNode, sorts it, and runs the visitor-based print() twice, even when both fields have no arguments. On the same document, base vs head: 300 repeated `b` fields went from 7.5 ms to 233.6 ms (31x), 2000 went from 230 ms to 10.5 s (46x), and 300 repeated `a(x:1, y:2)` fields went from 585 ms to 1595 ms (2.7x). Validation gets slower on every query that repeats a field name, and a crafted query buys much more server CPU per byte, in a rule whose previous bug (#3442) was already a denial-of-service hazard. The commit is titled as a simplification, not as a performance trade-off.
items.proposed_fix: Restore a cheap path in front of the printed comparison: take `args1`/`args2` as before, return a conflict when `args1.length !== args2.length`, treat two empty argument lists as equal without building or printing anything, and call `stringifyArguments` only when both fields have arguments. To also limit the cost with arguments, cache `stringifyArguments` results per FieldNode (for example in a WeakMap) so each node is printed once, not once per pair. Add a benchmark under benchmark/ for repeated same-name fields.

evidence: Removed base code: `if (arguments1.length !== arguments2.length) { return false; } return arguments1.every(...)`, which was a trivial true for two empty lists

Measured with the base and head src trees copied to a scratch dir (schema `type Query { a(x: Int, y: Int): Int b: Int }`, validate() with only this rule, average of 5 runs): noargs x300 base 7.49 ms / head 233.57 ms; args x300 base 584.75 ms / head 1595.11 ms; noargs x2000 base 230.10 ms / head 10542.72 ms

native_payload.intent: Simplify how OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule compares the arguments of two same-named fields: put all arguments in one synthetic ObjectValueNode, sort it, print it, and compare the strings, replacing the per-argument sameArguments/stringifyValue helpers. Which queries the rule accepts or rejects should not change.

residual_risks: Behavior change for documents that repeat an argument name (both reads found it; the adversarial reviewer rated it P3 at anchor 50). Old sameArguments used a first-match find(), so `{ f(a:1, a:1) f(a:1, a:2) }` passed while the reverse order failed. The new printed comparison reports 'they have differing arguments' in both orders. UniqueArgumentNamesRule already rejects these documents, so the effect is an extra, arguably more correct, error. The commit does not mention or test it.
testing_gaps: Nothing tests or benchmarks the cost of comparing many same-named fields with or without arguments. benchmark/ has no case that would have caught the 31x slowdown in finding #1.
No test pins the new symmetric handling of duplicate argument names (for example `{ f(a:1, a:1) f(a:1, a:2) }` should report differing arguments).

notes: Focused path: own correctness read plus one independent adversarial read. No other reviewer agents ran and no validator ran.

Adversarial lens: local in-process adversarial reviewer (same model family, Opus). The cross-model peer was skipped because the user prohibited external/other-model review. Agreement with it is not cross-model corroboration and promoted no confidence.
Finding #1 comes from the correctness read alone. It was verified by base-vs-head measurement and carries requires_verification for any fix.
